text: 30 October 2026 Global Market Outlook Download Report Transitioning to mid-cycle We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. We upgrade India to Overweight. Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over sovereign debt, but limit duration to 3-7 years. We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand. Where are the tactical opportunities? Are central banks likely to continue hiking rates? Are quantitative models still bullish on equities? Strategy Investment strategy and key themes Steve Brice Global Chief Investment Officer Manpreet Gill Chief Investment Officer, AMEE Raymond Cheng, CFA, CPA Chief Investment Officer, North Asia 12m Foundation Overweights: Gold US, Asia ex-Japan equities Emerging Market USD bonds Opportunistic ideas – Equities Global: High dividend US: Healthcare^ Euro area (EA): Banks, MSCI Switzerland^ Asia: Japan banks Top Global Sectors: US: Technology, healthcare^, financials, materials EA: Financials Asia: Japan financials Opportunistic ideas – Bonds US: Treasury Inflation-protected Securities (TIPS), AAA-rated collateralised loan obligations (CLOs), US High-yield (HY) Others: AUD corporates ^New Transitioning to mid-cycle We now favour a more balanced stance between stocks and bonds. Near-term event risks and high earnings expectations prompt us to trim equities to a Core holding. The US and Asia ex-Japan (AxJ) remain our preferred regions. Within AxJ, we upgrade India to Overweight. Higher bond yields are improving the outlook for future returns and offering increasingly attractive income opportunities. We are Overweight Emerging Market (EM) USD bonds and favour corporate over government bonds, but limit duration to 3-7 years. We remain Overweight gold. Prices are likely to grind higher as near-term headwinds from higher bond yields are offset by EM central bank demand. Great expectations Individual risk events, high earnings expectations and a higher cost of capital point to a more moderate return environment ahead. In the very near term, financial markets must navigate key event risks, such as (i) the US mid-term elections, which have historically been associated with elevated market volatility and (ii) renewed geopolitical tensions, with several reports suggesting the US is considering renewed strikes on Iran. These concerns have pushed the Brent oil price well above USD 110/bbl despite significant ongoing crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Higher bond yields combined with high earnings expectations raise the risk of an expectations reset. The US Q3 earnings season is attracting significant attention given high earnings expectations, particularly for the AI sector. However, higher US bond yields may start to bite as debt-financed capex takes on a greater share of total capex over the coming year. This, combined with already-high expectations, raises the risk of disappointment and a near-term repricing of expected earnings growth pace. Despite the current challenges, healthy growth continues to underpin the economic backdrop. The US economic outlook remains well supported, and the absolute level of year-ahead earnings expectations is high. We do not expect Fed rate hikes to result in overly restrictive policy. Our caution, thus, stems from the risk of an expectations repricing rather than an outright economic slowdown. Fig. 1 Our quant model score has fallen to levels associated with flat-to-modestly-negative equity returns Our quantitative stock-bond model Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered A more balanced stock-bond mix We trim global equities to a Core holding, leaving us Neutral on both equities and bonds and Overweight gold. The concerns laid out earlier point to near-term volatility risks and a somewhat lower long-term growth trajectory for equities. Our quant model also reflects this cautious outlook, having downgraded equities to a level usually associated with flat-to-modestly-negative returns. From a relative perspective, though, the higher yields on offer from bonds also raise the bar by presenting an increasingly compelling return outlook after several years of very low yields. We believe this argues for portfolios that are increasingly balanced between equities and bonds. Ways to diversify equity exposure We continue to favour global equity market diversification, with a preference for US and AxJ equities. We remain Overweight US and AxJ equities, expecting them to outperform other major regions. Earnings growth remains the main driver of this view – while growth rates could decelerate somewhat, we still expect them to remain higher than those of other major regions. Japan and Euro area equities remain attractive as regional diversifiers. Our positive view on both markets’ financial sectors supports our Core holding view on them. Within Asia, we are Overweight Taiwan and India. Indian equities have lagged the region this year, in part due to limited listed AI-related exposure. However, we believe this is increasingly likely to become an advantage as investors seek greater diversification away from excessive concentration in the AI theme. This comes at a time when the economic and earnings growth outlook for Indian equities is starting to improve. We retain a more Neutral view on Chinese equities amid a still-challenging growth outlook. We also favour greater sector diversification. In the US, we favour diversifying across our Overweight sectors of technology, financials, materials and healthcare. We also favour financials in Japan and the Euro area. Fig. 2 Negative gold-USD correlation has held back gold amid USD strength. This is unlikely to persist Gold and USD correlations over the last 15 years Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered Changes to our equity opportunistic ideas also reflect a more defensive stance. In recent weeks, we have closed our global semiconductors, MSCI Taiwan, US communication services and global power & electrification ideas and have opened new ideas on US healthcare and MSCI Switzerland. Riding the yield train We believe bond markets offer an attractive opportunity to lock in yields. The 10-year US government bond yield is now in a range last witnessed in 2007. While the process of rising yields results in lower bond prices – as painfully experienced in recent months – the yield level itself starts to significantly improve the outlook for future returns. Favour corporate over government bonds, but check your duration. Still-high credit quality means that we continue to favour taking on credit risk to earn a higher yield (EM USD bonds are preferred, but we also see investment-grade (IG) and high-yield (HY) bonds as Core holdings). However, limiting duration to 3-7 years remains key to avoiding excessive exposure to any inflation surprises. Changes to our bond opportunistic ideas also reflect a more balanced stance. We close our EU bank contingent convertible bonds (CoCos 2 – please refer page 27 ) and US utilities corporate hybrids ideas. We also close our opportunistic idea on US 10-year government bonds following the recent pullback in yields, locking in gains. Alternatives and gold to remain relevant Alternatives are an effective tool for portfolio risk management. Hedge funds and private markets provide a differentiated return stream, while rotating into alternatives helps reduce equity beta exposure. We examine downside capture and how beta is reduced via hedge fund sub-strategies and private markets in our asset allocation section. Gold remains a key Overweight. We trim our three- and 12-month forecasts modestly, but see gold forming a strong base above USD 4,000/oz. Rising bond yields and the USD were recent headwinds, but we expect a softer USD and continued EM central bank demand to result in 12-month gains. Foundation asset allocation models The Foundation and Foundation+ models are allocations that you can use as the starting point for building a diversified investment portfolio. The Foundation model showcases a set of allocations focusing on traditional asset classes that are accessible to most investors, while the Foundation+ model includes allocations to private assets that may be accessible to investors in some jurisdictions, but not others. Fig. 3 Foundation asset allocation for a balanced risk profile Fig. 4 Foundation+ asset allocation for a balanced risk profile Fig. 5 Multi-asset income allocation for a moderate risk profile Source: Standard Chartered Notes: (i) Developed Market (DM) IG Bonds is an aggregate of DM IG Government and DM IG Corporate Bonds; (ii) EM Bonds is an aggregate of EM USD and EM Local Ccy Government Bonds Foundation: Our tactical asset allocation views Fig. 6 Performance of our Foundation Allocations* Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered; *12-month performance data from 28 October 2025 to 28 October 2026, Six-month performance from 28 April 2026 to 28 October 2026, Three-month performance from 28 July 2026 to 28 October 2026 Fig. 7 Opportunistic ideas performance Macro overview – at a glance Rajat Bhattacharya Senior Investment Strategist Key themes Core scenario (soft landing, 45% probability): An economic soft landing remains our core scenario, with the global economy overcoming this year’s oil price shock thanks to a surge in AI investment in the US and Asia. Record wealth generation driven by the stock market rally is supporting US consumption. Fiscal easing in the US, Germany and Japan is supporting growth. Meanwhile, inflation has reaccelerated due to a rebound in fuel prices as the Middle East conflict drags on. Against this backdrop, the Fed, ECB and BoJ all hiked rates in the same month (in September) for the first time. Although all three subsequently paused in October, we expect the Fed to hike twice more, the ECB once more and the BoJ thrice more by June 2027. Nevertheless, we expect the energy and tariff effects on inflation to fade by H2 2027, enabling the Fed and the ECB to cut rates by Q3 2027. Meanwhile, China is likely to target credit easing and accelerate fiscal spending in H1 2027 to revive domestic growth. Upside risk (no landing, 30% probability): We maintain the probability at 30% as AI-driven investment growth continues. There is a reasonable chance that lower oil prices next year, the AI-fuelled wealth boom and fiscal easing in Germany and Japan will boost ‘animal spirits’. A potential global defence spending boom, led by the US and Europe, could also lift global growth. Downside risk (25% probability): We raised the risk of a recession to 15%, especially if central banks are forced to accelerate the pace of rate hikes to douse rising inflation. A stock market downturn negating the wealth effect or a bond sell-off due to fiscal concerns are other tail risks. We cut stagflation probability to 10% as we see low risk of oil prices sustaining above USD 120/bbl. Key chart The US-led AI-focused investment boom has lifted business confidence. The resulting equity market rally has boosted US household wealth, supporting consumption Fig. 8 Robust business confidence amid AI boom; equity rally lifts US household net worth Purchasing managers indices; US household net worth as percentage of personal disposable income Policy rates watch We expect the Fed to hike twice more by Q2 2027, then ease in H2 2027, as AI-led expansion continues. The US economy remains firmly in expansion. In Q3, annualised GDP growth accelerated to 3.4%, led by AI investments and consumption. In October, the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) remained strong at 57.6. Since our last monthly report, the consensus estimate for 2026 GDP growth has been nudged up to 2.3% from 2.1%, and the 2027 estimate has risen to 2.2%. That matches the Fed’s upgraded growth projection of 2.3% for 2026, but remains below the Fed’s 2.4% estimate for 2027. AI investment, fiscal support and household wealth are the main growth drivers, although consumer activity lags business spending. Higher bond yields and elevated oil prices are headwinds, but recession risks look contained. Our core scenario remains a ‘soft landing’, at 45%, with a meaningful 30% chance of a ‘no-landing’ upside. Rising gasoline and diesel prices pushed US core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation to 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, matching estimates. Consensus sees core PCE inflation slowing from 3.2% in Q4 2026 to 2.4% by Q4 2027 as energy and tariff effects fade. Underlying price momentum is softening, and recent PCE methodology revisions have lowered core inflation. However, fuel costs passed on to wider consumers and AI-driven chip shortages remain upside risks. In October, the Fed held rates at 4.0%, after hiking in September for the first time since 2023. We expect the Fed to hike rates by 25bps in December and 25bps more in H1 2027 due to elevated near-term energy inflation. It is likely to follow with a 25bps cut to 4.25% in Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This aligns with the Fed’s projected policy path, although it implies a more dovish trajectory than money markets, which are pricing another 56bps of hikes over the next 12 months. Political uncertainty after the mid-term election is a key risk. ECB to hike once more in December, then pause. The Euro area recovery is firming. GDP grew 1.2% y/y in Q2 2026, up from 0.6% in Q1, and the manufacturing PMI stayed robust at 52.4 in October. Consensus 2026 growth has been raised to 1.0% from 0.9%, and 2027 is unchanged at 1.3%. The main supports are resilient exports and German infrastructure and defence spending. However, cautious consumers and soft private investment limit the recovery, and energy costs are squeezing household incomes and business margins. Recession is not the central expectation. French fiscal stress and sustained high energy costs remain the key risks. Higher energy prices pushed Euro area headline inflation up to 3.8% y/y in September from 3.2% y/y in August, while core inflation rose to 2.5% y/y. Consensus expects headline and core inflation to ease to 2% y/y and 2.4% y/y by Q4 2027, respectively. Encouragingly, energy has had limited impact on core prices, and longer-term inflation expectations remain stable at around 2.1%. Together, these should allow inflation to moderate in 2027. The main risk is that energy, and especially gas, prices stay high for longer than expected. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% in October after raising it by 50bps this year. Inflation data continue to favour an additional hike in December. We expect an ECB rate hold in H1 2027, followed by a cut by Q3 2027 as disinflation returns. This policy path is more dovish than money markets, which are pricing more than 60bps of hikes over the next 12 months. China to provide targeted support to defend growth floor. China’s growth momentum recovered in September. Both the manufacturing PMI (50.1) and the non-manufacturing PMI (50.2) moved back into expansion. The construction PMI rose above 50 for the first time this year as infrastructure spending started to take effect. Exports grew 36.3% y/y, pushing the trade surplus to a record USD 133.5bn. We expect growth in 2026 to meet the lower end of the 4.5-5.0% target. Growth is increasingly bifurcated, though, with technology firms and exporters doing well, while household demand stays weak. Prices are rising again, but only narrowly. Consumer inflation edged up to 0.9% y/y in September, and producer inflation surged to 5% y/y, its highest since 2022, driven by energy and metals prices and concentrated in upstream sectors. With domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027. domestic demand weak and a high comparison base next year, the boost from energy prices is likely to fade in 2027. Policy is in ‘targeted easing’ mode. We expect a modest fiscal package to defend the growth floor rather than a large stimulus. The PBoC cut a key rate by 25bps to 1.5% to fund ‘Six Networks’ infrastructure projects and raised its relending quotas. A new interest subsidy on first-home mortgages provides limited support to demand. We expect no policy rate cut this year. There is still room to speed up fiscal spending, including by using CNY 500bn of unused local-government debt quota. If the PBoC switches to an overnight reverse repo rate as its policy rate, that would imply a de facto rate cut as the overnight rate is lower than the 7-day official policy rate. BoJ to hike at a quarterly pace until Q2 2027. Japan’s economy remains solid. Wages are growing above 4%, and the labour market is tight. The main headwind is high energy prices, which is slowing growth. Fiscal spending gives some support: the FY27 draft budget includes ambitious spending plans, alongside a proposed two-year cut to the consumption tax on food and a new five-year defence programme. However, this extra spending raises questions about fiscal sustainability. The BoJ unveiled plans to triple the pace of ETF sales from January 2027, potentially funding the tax cut. Price pressures now look firmly established. Headline and core inflation rose above 2% for the first time this year, and core-core inflation (ex-fresh food and energy) jumped to 2.4% and is expected to rise towards 3% in Q1 2027. Breakeven inflation rates have stayed above 2% most of this year. Real interest rates remain negative, hurting savers and pensioners. The BoJ held its policy rate at 1.25% in October, after raising it in September, only three months after its previous hike. This points to an accelerated quarterly hiking pace. We expect the quarterly pace of hikes to continue, taking the rate to 2% by June 2027. Money markets have caught up with our hawkish view in recent months. The BoJ noted for the first time that underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, marking a shift from creating inflation to containing it. Politics could slow the hiking cycle in H2 2027. Two government-appointed board members voted against the September hike, and the two most hawkish members are due to leave in July 2027. Fig. 9 Inflation is likely to ease globally by H2 2027 Consensus inflation estimates across major economies Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered Fig. 10 We expect limited central bank hikes over 12m Our estimates of key central bank policy rates over 12 months Asset classes Fixed Income – at a glance Jonathan Liang, CFA CIO, Fixed Income & FX Cedric Lam Senior Investment Strategist Ray Heung Senior Investment Strategist Anthony Naab, CFA Investment Strategist Our view Foundation: Bond yields remain near multi-year highs, offering an attractive entry point. We view fixed income as a Core holding (ie, a Neutral allocation) in our multi-asset portfolios. Within the asset class, we maintain an Overweight stance on EM USD government bonds, given their attractive risk-reward. We hold an Underweight view on Developed Market (DM) government bonds due to the tail risks associated with term premia. The Fed’s decision to hold rates at 3.75-4.00% in October amid still-elevated energy prices suggests that every Fed meeting from here is ‘live’, with a rate change possible on incoming data. With US inflation still running hot and the labour market tight, we expect two more 25bps hikes (one by year-end and one in H1 2027), bringing the Fed’s target range for the federal funds rate to 4.25-4.5%. We continue to favour the 3-7-year part of the US government bond yield curve as the best hedge against any risk-off move driven by AI-related growth fears. As inflation pressures ease in H2 2027, we see room for the Fed to consider a rate cut, which should pull nominal yields lower. Solid corporate fundamentals and supportive technicals should keep spreads tight, but there is limited room for them to tighten further. We still favour EM USD over local-currency (LCY) government bonds. Opportunistic ideas: We are bullish on US TIPS, AAA-rated CLOs, broad US HYs and Australian dollar (AUD) corporate bonds. Key charts Fig. 11 Rate forecasts and our view of bond classes DM rates – Underweight We remain Underweight DM government bonds. In the US, government bond yields have retraced meaningfully after a sharp bear steepening through September and early October. We expect real yields to stay elevated over the next six months as AI capex and productivity growth continue to drive above-trend economic growth. We expect two more 25bps rate hikes by June 2027. Over the next few months, we expect US government bond yields to remain rangebound. The near-term path hinges on five factors: 1) the 3 November US mid-term election, where a ‘Democratic sweep’ would likely be bond-supportive by constraining US President Trump’s fiscal spending agenda, while a ‘Republican sweep’ would likely weigh on bonds as markets price in further fiscal expansion and a higher term premium; 2) Fed communication at upcoming policy meetings; 3) the US Treasury’s quarterly refunding announcement on 4 November, where any signal of reduced long-end issuance would likely compress long-end yields; 4) softening auction demand and repatriation by foreign investors, which add uncertainty around demand for US government bonds; and 5) the fluid geopolitical situation in the Middle East, which is keeping oil prices elevated, with a risk of further upside. Going into H2 2027, we expect moderating oil prices and the fading inflationary impact of tariffs to give the Fed room to consider rate cuts. The US 30-year yield, however, is likely to stay elevated as fiscal deficit remains substantial next year. We expect a final ECB hike to 2.75% by December 2026, then a pause in H1 2027, followed by a 25bps cut in Q3 2027. In Japan, we expect quarterly pace of BoJ hikes, with one hike that takes the policy rate to 1.50% by December 2026 and two more in H1 2027, reaching 2.00% before pausing at mid-year. DM corporates – Core holding We maintain a Neutral allocation to both DM IG and DM HY corporate bonds, with a tactical bias to add exposure on episodic weakness, as carry continues to dominate total returns across DM credit. Credit spreads have widened from their lows but remain close to historical tights, while yields are still attractive, reinforcing a carry-led stance. This tight-spread regime is anchored by robust issuer fundamentals, strong profitability and resilient balance sheets, despite a visible moderation in rating upgrades over the past quarter. Technical supply dynamics are reshaping sector dispersion, especially in the IG space, where heavy AI-related issuance is weighing on the long end of the curve. AI-driven supply is surpassing USD 250bn in 2026 and making up a growing share of US IG gross issuance, but there are growing signs that hyperscalers are turning to private markets for funding, which should help ease public bond market supply pressures. We remain selective at the long end of the yield curve and favour a duration of 3-7 years, where risk-adjusted carry remains most durable. Issuance-driven concessions in sectors with strong capex cycles (notably technology, capital goods and basic industries) present opportunities for investors who can stomach near-term volatility. Fig. 12 DM IG spreads have widened from their lows, but remain near historically tight levels Bloomberg Global Aggregate Corp Index, option-adjusted spread (OAS) Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered DM HY spreads have widened to roughly a six-month high. Persistent doubts about whether hyperscalers can generate adequate returns on massive AI capex investments triggered a broad risk asset sell-off. The CCC tier has become the focal point of genuine credit concern, with yields hovering near the high-15% range and spreads near a four-year high. Market focus has shifted to the funding pressures facing AI-related neocloud companies. We view this as idiosyncratic for now and see a limited impact on the broader HY universe. The underlying credit picture is mixed. Leverage is elevated and interest coverage is thin, but the broad market has not yet shown signs of systemic stress. The US HY default rate remains below trend in 2026. HY offers an attractive income proposition, with all-in yields of over 8%. Its shorter-duration profile, combined with its lower sensitivity to changes in the term premium and rate volatility, make it an attractive sleeve in the current phase of the cycle. We remain attentive to evolving credit rating migration trends and sector-specific supply pressures, particularly as upgrades slow and new issuance clusters around key themes. However, healthy issuer fundamentals and stable credit metrics continue to support it as a Core holding allocation. Fig. 13 DM HY spreads are off the tights Bloomberg Global HY Aggregate Corporate Index, OAS Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered EM government bonds – Overweight USD/Core holding for LCY We are Overweight EM USD government bonds and retain EM LCY government bonds as a Core holding, reflecting a balanced perspective across both regional performance and currency dynamics. In EM USD sovereign debt, the recent spread widening offered an attractive entry point to gain exposure to areas benefiting from resilient global growth and stable external conditions. Technicals remain favourable, with supply being front-loaded and investor positioning remaining relatively light compared with historical levels. Many EM central banks having tightened earlier and more aggressively post-pandemic, preserving credibility and maintaining positive real rates. External balances have improved, reserve buffers have increased and greater reliance on domestic funding reduces external vulnerability. Lula’s surprise win in Brazil’s presidential election raises political risk. The country’s fiscal trajectory under the incoming administration is a key risk to monitor. Fiscal slippage could trigger a broader repricing of LATAM risk. In Asia, higher-rated issuers continue to offer a valuable buffer during bouts of global rate volatility, while select frontier exposures in EMEA remain more sensitive to liquidity shifts and changes in risk appetite. Index composition also shapes resilience: the EM USD benchmark is less exposed to oil price shocks, as countries that are not oil importers account for a larger share of the benchmark than in the LCY benchmark. We expect returns to be primarily driven by carry rather than further spread compression. Fig. 14 EM USD government bonds offer a yield pick-up of nearly 3ppt over DM peers Bloomberg EM USD Government Bond Index, yield to worst Source: Bloomberg, Standard Chartered EM LCY debt faces additional headwinds, especially as elevated US real yields and an appreciating USD dampen demand from foreign investors and reduce the comparative attractiveness of broad-based duration strategies. However, real yields remain comparatively supportive in several markets, and current valuations signal selective opportunities, especially given the restrictive monetary policy stances prevalent across many EM economies. Accordingly, EM LCY bonds retain their Core holding status, with portfolio emphasis placed on country selection and measured duration exposure, reflecting the differentiated currency dynamics at play. Key risks to both the USD and LCY segments include a potential escalation of the Middle East conflict, higher oil prices, renewed hawkishness from the Fed that could support further USD strength and weather-related disruptions, such as the effects of El Niño. Climate risks could prolong inflation pressures and hinder disinflation in vulnerable EM regions. Asia USD bonds – Core holding We retain a Neutral allocation to Asia USD bonds, an asset class that continues to reward investors with attractive nominal yields, favourable supply-demand technicals and robust credit fundamentals. Healthy corporate cash flows, low leverage and a high share of sovereign-linked issuers lend the segment a defensive quality relative to broader credit. The resilience has been evident year to date (YTD). Asia USD bonds have outperformed both DM government and DM IG corporate bonds on a total-return basis. We expect this relative strength to persist. The combination of carry and credit quality (over 60% of issues are sovereign or sovereign-related) anchors our conviction in the asset class, even as we maintain a Neutral stance. Equity – at a glance Sundeep Gantori, CFA, CAIA Chief Investment Officer, Equities Fook Hien Yap Senior Investment Strategist Cindy Lam, CFA Senior Investment Strategist Our view We downgrade global equities from Overweight to a Core allocation as we expect higher volatility in the near term. We expect this volatility to arise as equity market leadership broadens during the transition to a mid-cycle bull market . Equity returns will likely moderate from the 15-20% annualised range of the last few years but remain positive. We remain Overweight US and AxJ equities , which are expected to deliver the highest earnings growth in 2027 among the major regions. Within AxJ, we remain Overweight Taiwan , given structural AI-driven growth, and upgrade India to Overweight, for diversified non-AI growth exposure. South Korea is a Core holding, with attractive valuations but extreme volatility. China is also a Core holding, with attractive valuations but lacking a positive catalyst. We are Underweight ASEAN, which has a weaker growth profile. We maintain Japan as a Core holding as nominal growth supports broad-based earnings revisions. We also maintain a Core allocation to Europe ex-UK , which is enjoying an earnings recovery. We remain Underweight UK equities, given the market’s limited exposure to growth sectors. Key chart Earnings growth is driving gains in equities Fig. 15 Broad-based earnings strength is supporting global equities. Our Overweight views on AxJ and US equities are supported by robust earnings growth Shifting to a mid-cycle bull market The last few years have seen strong annual returns of 15-20% for global equities, consistent with the early cycle of a bull market, driven in large part by a rapid AI buildout. As the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly debt funded – we estimate 40% of AI capex in 2027 would be debt-financed – the market is increasingly concerned about the quality of this growth and execution risks. We remain positive on the structural AI theme, but we expect investor focus to shift from rapid buildout to monetisation. During this transition, we expect market leadership to broaden beyond technology. We believe this shift will also be accompanied by higher near-term volatility and a moderation in global equity returns , consistent with a transition to a mid-cycle bull market. Fig. 16 Projected 16% earnings growth for global equities in 2027 provides a strong tailwind for positive equity returns 2026 and 2027 consensus earnings growth estimates for MSCI AC World sectors Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered US equities – Overweight US equity valuations have declined this year , with the 12-month forward P/E falling to 19x from 22x at the start of the year. This reflects higher rates, a valuation headwind, and worries about the quality of growth, which is increasingly debt-funded. As market leadership broadens and the US mid-term election nears, we expect higher near-term volatility in the US market. Nonetheless, US equities have broad-based strength, with the ongoing Q3 earnings season pointing to a robust economy. In a world of rising geopolitical risks, the US is also relatively insulated by its domestically driven growth. AxJ equities – Overweight AxJ has the strongest earnings growth among major markets, as its technology sector remains a key beneficiary of the AI capex cycle. AxJ’s P/E valuations have also dropped to attractive trough levels, the lowest among major regions. Within AxJ, we are Overweight Taiwan , which benefits from clear visibility on AI-driven growth and dominance in manufacturing advanced AI chips. We also upgrade India to Overweight due to its resilient domestically driven earnings, providing diversification beyond AI-related growth. India offers the highest exposure to defensive sectors (healthcare, consumer staples and utilities) within AxJ. Both Taiwan and India offer attractive returns on equity. South Korea equities remain a Core holding. We are positive on long-term agreements that improve earnings visibility for memory chipmakers. Valuations are attractive (the lowest in AxJ), with supportive corporate governance reforms. Still, extreme volatility remains the key overhang. China remains a Core holding, given inexpensive valuations, but re-rating potential appears delayed amid AI monetisation struggles, lingering regulatory risks and weak domestic demand. We remain Underweight ASEAN , as Indonesia’s downgrade warning, oil shocks and a well-supported USD could weigh on the region, although Singapore offers defensive growth. Fig. 17 India offers highest AxJ exposure to defensive sectors (healthcare, consumer staples and utilities) Sector weights for MSCI equity indices Source: FactSet, Bloomberg, Standard Chartered Japan equities – Core holding Rising nominal growth is supporting solid broad-based earnings revisions , with rising rates supportive of bank earnings. Corporate governance reforms also continue to boost shareholder value. The fiscal support for strategic industries is pro-growth, offsetting energy shocks. Europe ex-UK equities – Core holding Europe ex-UK is seeing an earnings recovery after three stagnant years, and we expect to see a continuation of this narrative with Q3 results. Rising rates are supportive of banks’ earnings and fiscal expansion is benefiting domestic demand. The fiscal situation in France has no easy solution, but we do not expect a contagion widening in government bond spreads, as the ECB has tools in place to limit contagion. UK equities – Underweight The UK lacks exposure to growth sectors, with relatively muted earnings growth. We expect this to weigh on the UK, making it lag the performance of other markets over the next 12 months, although UK equities tend to hold up better during bouts of volatility. Equity opportunistic views Robin Xie, CFA Senior Investment Strategist Ryan Goh Investment Strategist Jason Wong Equity Analyst Add MSCI Switzerland and US Healthcare, remove Global Power & Electrification, MSCI Taiwan, Global Semis and US Comm Services We initiate an opportunistic Idea on MSCI Switzerland on 29 October 2026, having initiated one on US Healthcare on 12 October 2026. Healthcare and Consumer Staples account for over 50% of the MSCI Switzerland Index’s weight, providing exposure to more resilient demand. It also has a sizeable financial sector supported by steady wealth management growth and well-capitalised insurers, which benefit from disciplined underwriting and resilient premium income. We closed our opportunistic ideas in Global Semiconductors (9 September 2026 to 2 October 2026: +8.1%), MSCI Taiwan (9 July 2026 to 2 October 2026: +10.0%), US Communication Services (18 June 2026 to 12 October 2026: +1.9%), and Global Power & Electrification (30 July 2026 to 29 October 2026: -6.5%). This reflects a tactical reduction in exposure to tech-related sectors amid higher expected near-term volatility, rather than a deterioration in the fundamental outlook. Over the longer term, we remain constructive on these structural themes and may revisit these ideas at more attractive entry points. Fig. 19 Opportunistic ideas Ongoing Opportunistic Ideas US Healthcare: We expect US Healthcare to offer resilience amid shifting market leadership, with the sector projected to grow by 23% in 2027, the second-fastest growth rate among MSCI US sectors, underpinned by healthcare innovation. Euro area banks: A ‘higher-for-longer’ rate backdrop should extend the earnings upcycle, with further ECB tightening expected. Corporate loan demand is showing recovery, while non-interest income is growing. Strong capital generation supports higher dividends and continued share buybacks. Japan Banks: BoJ policy normalisation drives net interest margin upside, while Japan’s reflation cycle supports nominal loan demand, corporate capex and household wealth activity. Governance reform is a re-rating driver independent of the rate cycle. This includes recycling legacy holdings towards growth, buybacks and dividends. Global High Dividend: Provides a higher-income equity allocation with historically lower volatility than the MSCI ACWI and modest downside cushioning on balance. Sector views: Continue to broaden & diversify We made two changes on 12 October 2026: we downgraded US Communication Services to Neutral to reduce concentration in tech-related sectors and upgraded US Healthcare to Overweight, where its defensive exposure stands to benefit as investors diversify beyond concentrated AI exposure. This month, we downgrade Europe ex-UK Industrials to Neutral , as energy-cost shocks and supply-chain pressures outweigh fiscal support. Elsewhere, US Information Technology (IT) remains Overweight. Rising funding and execution risks warrant near-term caution, but structural AI tailwinds should continue to provide long-term growth opportunities. US Materials also stays Overweight on sustained demand for industrial metals and construction materials. We remain bullish on gold. The Financial sector remains Overweight across the US, Europe ex-UK and Japan , supported by stable earnings, elevated rates boosting net interest income and continued capital market recovery. In China, we maintain a broad Overweight stance to preserve sector diversification. IT and Communication Services remain Overweight , with rapid innovation and investment in AI localisation providing tailwinds. Beyond these, we are also Overweight Materials on structurally elevated commodity prices, Healthcare on biotech innovation and a robust drug pipeline and the Financial sector on easing margin pressure, recovering fee income and capital market reform. We retain our three- and 12-month West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil forecast at USD 100/bbl and USD 80/bbl, respectively. USD strength is a headwind, but gold’s sensitivity to real yields has eased amid continued central bank buying, led by China, and resilient investor demand. FX – at a glance Jonathan Liang, CFA CIO, Fixed Income & FX <strong>Vincent Tan</strong> Senior Investment Strategist Iris Yuen Investment Strategist USD view USD consolidation with limited upside: Our three-month US Dollar Index (DXY) forecast stands at 101, revised upwards from 100.20 last month, reflecting a higher expected Fed rate path. With the October Fed rate pause and a potential December rate hike largely priced in, further tightening would offer limited additional USD support. Persistent inflation, elevated US government bond yields and resilient business activity continue to underpin the USD’s interest-rate advantage. However, in September, payroll growth slowed sharply to 29,000 (from 133,000 in August), the unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, annual wage growth eased to 3.0% from 3.1% and housing starts fell 5.2% m/m. These signs of cooling demand temper expectations of more aggressive Fed tightening. We expect DXY to remain rangebound between 101 and 103, with our three-month forecast at 101.00. Peaking Fed rates and narrowing rate differentials favour gradual USD weakness: We maintain our 12-month DXY forecast at 98.50. We expect a Fed rate hike in December 2026 and another in H1 2027, taking the federal funds target range to a peak of 4.25-4.50%, before easing in H2 2027. Further BoJ normalisation and the ECB’s relatively restrictive policy stance should progressively narrow the USD’s rate advantage. Persistent fiscal and current account deficits increase reliance on foreign capital inflows, adding to medium-term pressure on the USD. Resilient US growth, AI-related capital inflows and elevated US government bond yields remain important offsets, supporting DXY’s gradual decline towards 98.50. Historically, a decline in the model score to -2 has been associated with flat to slightly negative returns. The shift was driven by stretched valuations in both global and Asian equities, weaker fundamentals and deteriorating market technicals. On fundamentals, market risk aversion has risen sharply, while PMI new orders have declined over the past three months, pointing to a slowdown in the pace of industrial expansion. On technicals, the share of equity markets trading above their 200-day moving averages, a key gauge of long-term support, has fallen below 60% for the first time since January 2025. The model rebalances in the middle of each month and has generated 11bps of alpha from the equity Underweight initiated on 15 October 2026, lifting YTD alpha vs. the 60/40 equity-bond benchmark to 4.0%. Our 1-3-month equity market regime model indicates contained bear market risks across US and global equities. Estimated bear market probabilities are 4.2% for the S&P500 and 7.7% for the MSCI AC World, compared with 0.9% and 6.4% respectively in the September outlook. Across both models, volatility measures are the main factors keeping probabilities low, supported by momentum signals. Together, these outweigh modest upward contributions from macro and cross-market factors, leaving little evidence of a bear market regime over the next 1-3 months. Our market diversity indicator flags reversal risk in MSCI Europe Real Estate and MSCI China Industrials, which are down over 12% and 19% respectively from their August peaks. US equity and USD positioning remain broadly neutral.
